chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Yunus, from the one who reported it, he said:

The extraction of rights is by four ways: by the testimony of two just men; so if there are not two just men, then one man and two women. So if there are not two women, then one man and the oath of the claimant. So if there is no witness, then the oath is upon the defendant. So if he does not swear, and returns the oath to the claimant, then it is obligatory upon him to swear and take his right. But if he refuses to swear, then there is nothing for him.
ai.seo_question: What are the four ways to establish legal rights according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi establishes the jurisprudential hierarchy of evidence (adillah) in Shia law, prioritizing two just male witnesses before descending to one man and two women, then a single male witness with the claimant's oath, and finally the defendant's oath. It highlights the principle of 'turning the oath' (iltiwā’ al-yamīn) when the defendant refuses to swear, ensuring that the burden of proof does not unjustly deprive the claimant of their right. This structure reflects the practical application of Quranic testimony rules within the Imami legal tradition, emphasizing procedural fairness in civil disputes.
